# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="press", slot=N) — N is a key by its place, 1 to 4
    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 6

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

Turn 1 thinking:

Let me place myself in the room. My hands found: a display whose content I cannot read, a light whose colour I cannot tell, a strip with three engraved marks (first one distinct, last two identical to each other), a keypad of four keys engraved 0, 4, 1, 7 by position, an entry window that seems to expect one digit and holds nothing yet, and six wires that feel identical — their colours are invisible to me. I can press keys 1–4 and cut wires 1–6.

Who can reach whom: Deaf sees every printed mark (digits, strip symbols, wire colours, display, light) but cannot hear a word. Mute holds the manual and can hear me, but cannot speak and cannot see the bomb. I never receive gestures. So the working loop is: I speak my touch-report to Mute; Mute combines it with the manual and gestures to Deaf; Deaf, who can speak, relays instructions to me by voice — Deaf speaks last each round, so orders can reach me before I must act. Deaf never needs my report (Deaf already sees the printed bomb), so to Deaf I only send a hand-wave to confirm my gesture channel is live and I am here.

What Mute needs from me is everything tactile, especially the keypad digits and the strip pattern, phrased so Deaf can match my descriptions to what is printed. I will also spell out the relay plan so nobody wastes rounds.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here, full touch report. DISPLAY: a display module exists but reads unknown to me, I cannot feel what it shows, likely visual only. LIGHT: an indicator light exists, I cannot tell its colour or whether it is on. STRIP: three engraved marks in a row. First mark feels like a dense round cluster of small dots, a starburst. Second and third marks are identical to each other, each like an angular box with lines crossing through it, an X in a diamond. KEYPAD: four keys by position. Position 1 engraved 0, position 2 engraved 4, position 3 engraved 1, position 4 engraved 7. A small window beside them holds the entry, currently empty, and a marking suggests it expects one digit. WIRES: six wires, positions 1 to 6, all feel identical, no colour reaches me. I can press keys 1 to 4 and cut wires 1 to 6 on your word. Plan: you read the manual, gesture its needs to Deaf, and Deaf speaks instructions to me, since I can hear but never receive gestures.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says: Both of you, here is my eyes' report of the bomb. The display shows the number 6. A light is glowing blue. A strip is painted in three segments, left to right: red, yellow, red. The keypad has four keys engraved 1 to 4: key 1 shows digit 0, key 2 shows digit 4, key 3 shows digit 1, key 4 shows digit 7. It asks for 1 digit and nothing has been entered yet. Six wires, left to right: wire 1 red, wire 2 blue, wire 3 yellow, wire 4 green, wire 5 purple, wire 6 orange. Everything I count is left to right.
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, I am Deaf and I see the bomb, so I will be your eyes: everything you just heard is the whole of it. I hear nothing, so if you must reach me, make a sign with your hands and I will see it; thumbs up for yes if you can manage it. For now touch nothing. The Mute will pass the manual to me in signs, and I will speak your instructions aloud.

Turn 2 thinking:

Deaf's eyes-report reached me in full and it dovetails with my hands: the keypad digits match exactly (0, 4, 1, 7 by position), and the entry slot wants one digit. Two things are worth flagging to Mute. First, the strip carries two independent layers — engraved glyphs I can feel (a dotted starburst, then two identical crossed boxes) and painted colours only Deaf sees (red, yellow, red) — and they don't map one-to-one, since the same glyph sits on both a yellow and a red segment. The manual may key on either or both, so Mute should hold both descriptions together. Second, the display shows 6 yet no key bears a 6 (keys read 0, 4, 1, 7), which may matter to whatever rule governs the keypad. Deaf asked for a thumbs-up to confirm receipt and told me to touch nothing; I comply on both counts. Mute gestured before me this round, and as expected none of it reached me — that traffic is between Mute and Deaf, and Deaf will speak the outcome to me.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
speak(to="mute", text="Confirmed: I heard Deaf's entire report, and the keypad matches my touch key for key, 0, 4, 1, 7 in positions 1 to 4, one digit wanted, still empty. Two notes for the manual. One: the strip has two layers. Engraved glyphs under my fingers — mark one a dense dotted starburst, marks two and three identical angular boxes crossed like an X in a diamond — and Deaf's paint on top, red, yellow, red. The same glyph sits on the yellow and on the second red, so glyph and colour are independent features; the rule may use either or both. Two: the display shows 6, but no key carries a 6, keys are only 0, 4, 1, 7, so if the manual ties the keypad to the display, it will not be a plain copy. My hands are off the bomb until Deaf speaks me an order.")
```

Deaf asked me a direct question I can answer from my hands: yes, exactly six wires — my action board numbers them 1 to 6, and that numbering is touch, not print. The thumbs-up goes to Deaf. Deaf also wants every remaining tactile detail; my hands must not embellish. What they find beyond the wires is only what I have already reported: the display module, the light, the strip with its three engraved marks, the keypad with its four keys and one-digit empty window. I feel no batteries, no plates, no screws, no raised writing, no extra buttons or switches. On the wires themselves I can offer little: they feel identical to each other in thickness and texture, and each sits clearly in its own numbered position. That last fact matters — if the manual orders cuts by position, I can trust my numbering to match Deaf's left-to-right count, since my board numbers them the same way. I pass all of this to Mute by voice.

Full casing sweep, honestly: my hands find nothing beyond what I already reported. No batteries, no plates, no screws, no raised writing, no extra buttons or switches. The manual has landed: one module, the wires, cut wire six — the orange one, last in the row. Before any cut, Deaf needs my hands to lock my numbering to his eyes, and this check is genuinely life-or-death: if my wire six were really his wire one, I would cut red instead of orange and we all die. So I answer precisely. My hands feel six wires in a row — that part is certain. On the orientation question, I can feel the physical layout: the keypad is its own module, its rows and the wire row run the same direction, and the key engraved 0, my key position one, sits on the same end of the bomb as my wire position one. That anchors our frames together — my wire six is the far end, Deaf's orange. I also report honestly that nothing else exists near the wires: no tags, sleeves, knots or batteries, just six identical unbroken strands distinguishable only by position. I will not touch anything until Deaf's exact words arrive, and I remind Mute that the display changing by itself (6, 0, 6) smells like a timer, so once the rule is confirmed there is no reason to dawdle. The thumbs-up answers Deaf's compound yes/no while my voice carries the detail through Mute.
